data.raw_text:
After watching yesterday’s so-called “anti-corruption” rally in Metro Manila, it’s clear there were several types of people showing up and speaking out:

• Those shouting “Marcos Resign.”
They claim to stand on principle, but most can’t point to a specific, verifiable act that merits resignation—only vague grievances and recycled narratives fed to them.

• Those demanding “Marcos and Sara Resign.”
They insist they’re fighting dynasties and incompetence, yet their talking points shift depending on who’s steering the outrage that day. Worse, it’s the exact same slogan from 40 years ago—no plan, no roadmap, no understanding of who or what would take over if their fantasy happened.

• Those marching under the flag of anti-corruption.
A noble cause in theory—but many can’t name a concrete corruption case tied to the current administration. What you hear instead are old accusations, generalized anger, and slogans held together by emotion rather than evidence.

• Those chanting “accountability and transparency.”
Great words, empty context. Their messaging is scattered, inconsistent, and rarely grounded in actionable issues. Reality check: several individuals are already indicted or behind bars—with more cases moving forward.

• Those craving something “historic” or dramatic in their lives.
For them, the rally isn’t about governance at all; it’s about being part of a spectacle, collecting photos and videos they can post online to feel like they witnessed a turning point.

• And then the crowd fillers—those who simply have nothing better to do.
People who tag along out of boredom, FOMO, or peer pressure, contributing nothing but headcount and noise.

Put all of these groups together and you get a crowd moving in every direction at once. No unified purpose, no coherent message—just a chaotic mix of motives and muddled narratives. That’s why the whole rally felt less like a principled movement and more like a confused gathering pretending to stand for something it can’t even define.
